title: Genomic analysis of high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses from Antarctica reveals multiple introductions from South America

paper_content.abstract: The spread of high pathogenic avian influenza virus (HPAIV) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into Antarctica poses a major threat to polar wildlife. We report the detection of H5N1 in carcasses of eight species during the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 austral summers in the South Shetland Islands: Antarctic shag, Antarctic tern, kelp gull, pintado petrel, Antarctic petrel, skuas, Antarctic fur seal, and southern elephant seal. Whole-genome sequencing, mutational profiling, and phylogenetic reconstruction revealed that the viruses detected in these hosts descended from distinct introduction events. One group of strains including complete and partial viral genomes from a gull, skuas, fur seals, an Antarctic tern, and a southern elephant seal clustered with H5N1 strains previously detected in marine mammals in South America and formed a polyphyletic lineage consistent with at least two independent introductions into Antarctica. A second group of strains including complete and partial viral genomes from petrels, shags, and skuas clustered with H5N1 strains previously detected in seabirds and marine mammals in South Georgia and with a previously reported HPAIV detection from Torgersen Island, Antarctic Peninsula. These findings reveal extensive epidemiological connectivity between South America and Antarctica, with South Georgia serving as a “stepping stone” for virus spread in the region.
paper_content.introduction:
Global spread of the high pathogenicity avian influenza virus (HPAIV) subtype H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b has caused unprecedented mortality among wild animals1. In late 2022, viruses of the B3.2 genotype were introduced to the Pacific coast of South America, disseminating rapidly and causing outbreaks in poultry and wildlife2–4. Phylogenetic reconstruction reveals that shortly after arrival to South America these viruses diverged into two sub-clades: an “avian” sub-clade that spread inland and was detected predominantly in poultry and terrestrial wild birds, and a “marine mammal” sub-clade that spread coastally and was detected predominantly in marine mammals and seabirds5,6. In October and November 2023, HPAIV H5N1 spread from South America onto the Subantarctic region, causing outbreaks in seabirds and marine mammals in South Georgia and Falkland (Malvinas) Islands7. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the viruses from South Georgia were monophyletic, descending from the South American “avian” sub-clade, whereas the strains from the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands were polyphyletic, descending from the South American “marine mammal” sub-clade7.

As the virus disseminated in wildlife in South America and South Georgia, concerns were raised that it could spread further onto the Antarctic Peninsula8,9. The first reports of wildlife mortality suspected to be due to HPAIV H5N1 in the Antarctic region were made in December 202310, and several confirmed detections have been made along the Antarctic Peninsula since then10–13. During the austral summers of 2023/2024 and 2024/2025, we collected swabs and tissue samples from deceased wildlife in the South Shetland Islands, Antarctic Peninsula, to perform molecular testing and genomic characterization of HPAIV H5N1.
paper_content.results:
We tested tissue and swab samples from 31 carcasses from 11 species (Supplementary Table 1), with 18 carcasses from 8 species testing positive for H5 influenza A virus: Antarctic shag (Leucocarbo bransfieldensis), Antarctic tern (Sterna vittata), kelp gull (Larus dominicanus), pintado petrel (Daption capense), Antarctic petrel (Thalassoica antarctica), skua (Stercorarius sp.), Antarctic fur seal (Arctocephalus gazella), and southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina). In total, 18 complete genomes (from 12 individuals) and 7 partial genomes (from 6 individuals) were recovered (Table 1). A maximum likelihood tree for the HA gene segment including globally-representative Gs/Gd clade 2.3.4.4b strains during 2021–2024 revealed that all viruses detected in the Subantarctic and Antarctic region to date stem from the viruses that circulated in South America since 2022 (Supplementary Figure 1). Furthermore, all complete genomes were of the H5N1 subtype with the B3.2 genotype; partial genomes were also in agreement with this classification.

Phylogenetic reconstructions of the concatenated whole genomes indicated the viruses recovered in this study belong to two clearly distinct groups, “a” and “b” (Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 2). Phylogenetic group “a” comprised 10 complete genomes (recovered from 3 Antarctic fur seals, 1 kelp gull, and 3 skuas) that clustered with viruses previously detected predominantly in marine mammals in South America (i.e. the South American “marine mammal” sub-clade2). Sequence identity suggests that 6 partial genomes (recovered from 1 Antarctic tern, 2 skuas, 1 Antarctic petrel, 1 southern elephant seal) were also part of this group. Phylogenetic reconstruction of concatenated whole genomes suggestRed that this group could be further divided into four subgroups, each potentially descending from a separate introduction event to Antarctica (Figure 1a). However, separate phylogenetic analysis of the longer gene segments (PB2, PB1, PA, HA, NP) only corroborated three subgroups, whereas analysis of the shorter gene segments only corroborated one (MP) or two subgroups (NA, NS) (Supplementary Figure 3).

On the other hand, phylogenetic group “b” (Figure 1b) comprised 8 complete genomes (recovered from 1 Antarctic shag, 1 pintado petrel, and 3 skuas) clustered with viruses previously detected in seabirds and marine mammals from South Georgia and with a previously reported HPAIV detection in a brown skua (Stercorarius antarcticus) from Torgersen Island in Antarctica, which in turn descended from viruses that circulated in poultry and wild birds in South America (i.e. the South American “avian” sub-clade2). Sequence identity suggests that one partial genome (recovered from Antarctic shag) was also part of this group. This group was consistently monophyletic across all phylogenetic reconstructions (Supplementary Figures 2 and 3), suggesting that these viruses and the Torgersen Island virus descended from a single introduction event to Antarctica.

A comparison of cycle threshold (Ct) values of the Real Time RT-PCR revealed that birds could be classified as either oral shedders, which had higher viral loads (i.e. lower Ct values) in the oropharyngeal swabs than in the cloacal swabs, or fecal shedders, which had higher viral loads in cloacal swabs than in oropharyngeal swabs. Birds infected with group “a” strains were more frequently oral shedders (2 skuas, 1 tern) than fecal shedders (1 skua), whereas birds infected with group “b” strains were more frequently fecal shedders (1 skua, 1 petrel) than oral shedders (1 skua) (Supplementary Figure 4).

Mutational analysis revealed amino acid substitutions that distinguished phylogenetic groups “a” and “b” across all proteins except M1 (Figure 2 and Supplementary Data 1). Most group “a” strains recovered from both birds and mammals showed two key mammalian adaptation substitutions in PB2 (PB2-Q591K and PB2-D701N); another mammalian adaptation substitution in NP (NP-N319K) was detected in a group “a” strain recovered from the brain of an Antarctic fur seal (individual O2904). All group “b” viruses had a deletion of 17 amino acids in the neuraminidase stalk (positions 58-74). Lastly, two amino acid motifs were observed in the hemagglutinin cleavage site. The original PLREKRRKRGLF motif was found in most viruses from both phylogenetic groups, comprising 14 complete genomes and 5 partial genomes. However, the PLKEKRRKRGLF motif was detected in group “a” viruses recovered from three hosts: one Antarctic fur seal (three complete genomes from the same individual), one Antarctic tern (one partial genome), and one Antarctic petrel (one partial genome) (Supplementary Table 2).
paper_content.methods:
Sample collection
This study was conducted in compliance with all relevant ethical and environmental regulations. No live animals were handled or sampled, as all biological material was obtained from carcasses. Research activities were carried out under license LW-20/24 issued by the Animal Use Ethics Committee of the Vice-Presidency for Research and Biological Collections (VPPCB), Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (Fiocruz). Sampling activities in Antarctica were authorized by the Environmental Assessment Group of the Brazilian Antarctic Program (PROANTAR). Fieldwork was conducted within the framework of the FIOANTAR and VIDEANTAR projects, with logistical support provided by the Brazilian Navy. All procedures followed strict biosafety protocols to ensure sample integrity and researcher safety. Supplementary Table 1 provides detailed information on the animals sampled. Oropharyngeal, oral, nasal, and cloacal swabs and brain tissue samples were collected in tubes with 1 mL of DNA/RNA Shield (Zymo Research, Irvine, USA) and stored at –80ºC. Samples were then transported with a strict cold-chain to the Laboratory of Respiratory Viruses, Exanthematous, Enteroviruses, and Viral Emergencies at the Oswaldo Cruz Institute (IOC) for further analysis.

RNA extraction and real-time RT-PCR
RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Cat. No. 52906) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Detection and subtyping of influenza A virus were performed by real-time RT-PCR using two assays: (i) the Biomanguinhos INFA/INFB/SC2 Multiplex Kit (ANVISA Registration No. 8014217006095), and (ii) the CDC Influenza A/B Typing Panel (Flu A/B Typing Kit, Cat. No. FluIVD03-6), targeting the matrix (InfA) and hemagglutinin (H5a and H5b) genes46,47 (Supplementary Data 1). H5a was developed to detect specific groups of H5 viruses of Asian origin (A/goose/Guangdong/1996 lineage and derivatives, which include many HPAI strains). H5b is complementary, covering genetic variations of H5 that could escape detection by the H5a assay. A viral load index was calculated for each sample by subtracting the Cycle threshold (Ct) value from 40.

Whole-genome sequencing and assembly
Whole-genome sequencing of positive samples was performed using a Multisegment Reverse Transcription-PCR (M-RT-PCR) amplification protocol48,49. The sequencing library was constructed using the COVIDSeq kit (Illumina, San Diego, USA). Sequencing was conducted on the MiSeq platform (Illumina), and genome assembly was carried out using the Iterative Refinement Meta-Assembler (IRMA) pipeline50. Clade classification was performed using NextClade v3.10.1 (https://clades.nextstrain.org/).

Bayesian evolutionary analysis
To place the viruses recovered from Antarctic wildlife in a global context, we downloaded 822 globally-representative HA gene sequences from Gs/Gd clade 2.3.4.4b viruses during 2021–2024 using NextStrain (https://nextstrain.org/). Phylogenetic relationships were inferred for the HA gene using the Maximum Likelihood methods available in IQ-Tree v. 2.4.0 with a GTR model of nucleotide substitution with gamma-distributed rate variation among sites. Publicly-available sequences of influenza A viruses from South America and Antarctica were obtained through Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data - GISAID (https://www.gisaid.org/) and GenBank (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nucleotide/) (Supplementary Data 2). Because this initial analysis confirmed that all Antarctic/Subantarctic strains were descendent from South American strains, subsequent evolutionary analyses omitted viruses from other continents. The temporal structure of the datasets in each segment was evaluated using TempEst v1.5.351 through a root-to-tip linear regression. The significance of the correlation between collection date and genetic distance was assessed using a Pearson correlation test, with adjustments for multiple comparisons made via the Benjamini–Hochberg method for false discovery rate control. Time-scaled phylogenetic trees were estimated using the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach implemented in BEAST v1.10.452, with BEAGLE v4.0.053 to improve computational efficiency. Bayesian trees were reconstructed under the nucleotide substitution model selected by jModelTest v2.1.1054, the non-parametric Bayesian Skyline coalescent demographic model55, and a relaxed molecular clock model with a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) rate reference prior56. The molecular clock, the time to the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA), and the spatial dynamics of each viral segment were reconstructed using a discrete phylogeographic model57 implemented in BEAST v1.10.4. A symmetric diffusion model was intentionally adopted as a conservative framework, allowing directional patterns of viral spread to emerge from the data rather than being imposed by prior assumptions, particularly given the limited and uneven geographic sampling in Antarctica.

In addition to segment-based analyses, concatenated gene datasets were also constructed and evaluated under the same Bayesian phylogeographic framework to capture genome-wide evolutionary signals. Sequences were coded according to both their sampling locations and host. For each dataset, independent MCMC runs were performed and subsequently combined to confirm that all continuous parameters achieved an effective sample size (ESS) greater than 100–200, as verified using Tracer v1.758. The maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree was summarized with TreeAnnotator v1.1052. Trees were visualized using R v4.4.159 with the packages treeio v1.30.060 and ggtree v3.14.061.

Mutational analysis
The translated sequence of all eight gene segments were compared to evaluate the presence of amino acid substitutions using NextClade v3.10.1 (https://clades.nextstrain.org/). An early B3.2 genotype strain (A/turkey/South Dakota/22-008485-001/2022; GISAID accession code EPI_ISL_11971481)62 was used as a reference.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Here the authors present PCR detection and sequencing of sequencing of H5N1 virus from 3 animals on 2 Antarctic islands.
Unfortunately, the presented results to not provide robust support for the conclusions.
There are major problems with this manuscript. Only 7 carcasses were sampled. The sample numbers are so small that only
the most simple conclusions could be made, particularly as the phylogenetic analysis is limited. For example, the authors
restrict their analysis to H5 sequences from South America and Antrarctica without any justification. And overall the datasets
are not adequately described. The authors also describe phylogeographic analysis in the methods, but these are not
presented in the manuscript.
Despite these major flaws, the authors are making sweeping statements about the movement of the virus throughout South
America and into Antarctica. There is no support provided for statements such as “Our phylogenetic results support the
growing evidence that South Georgia has played a significant role as a “stepping stone” for the spread of HPAIV in the
Subantarctic and Antarctic region”.
Overall this study lacks substance and significance. Sampling size is incredibly small and inadequate and just 3 new
genomes were generated in this study. This manuscript does not provide any new insights into the spread of H5N1 virus into
wild animal populations or into Antarctica.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript presents data on the recent detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in Antarctic wildlife,
including viral genome sequences suggesting several independent introductions of the virus into Antarctica. The manuscript
is overall well written and the results are clear and of timely significance. There are however some points that could be
clarified.
Major comments:
Line 231 - Please clarify which primers were used as in the cited reference they present several primers, and I did not find
any obvious mention of the “H5a” and “H5b” labels.
Figure 1 - Please explain the rationale for using PB2 opposed to other segments?
Can you explain why you did not use a concatenated genome (after removing reassortants) for improved resolution as Uhart
et al., 2024, and Clessin et al., 2025 did? Also why you used a model assuming symmetric dissemination (line 257) when
the expectation is that the virus was at the time spreading mostly Southwards?
I would suggest toning down the conclusion about the direct introductions from South America (e.g., line 99; header line 111,
remove “directly”) as it is pointed out several times in the manuscript that data is sparse, and notably we have no idea of
what is happening at sea, and considering how long the branches are on the phylogenetic tree.
The focus on biosecurity in the context of human movement (lines 49, 198 and 212) feels disconnected from the results
given that animal movements are suspected to be responsible for spread (e.g., discussed in line 176).
Minor comments:
Line 68 - Would it be possible to include information on the number of tested samples (instead of only the ones that returned
positive) here? E.g., a reference to Supplementary File 2. This could help build knowledge over the likelyhood to detect the
virus in the system.
Lines 228-232 - Please clarify product # when possible (Qiagen kit, Biomanguinhos INFA/INFB/SC2 kit, CDC Influenza A
kit…)
Lines 230-232 - Says “detection and subtyping were performed” two times with different methods. Please clarify.
Figure 1 - Posterior probability for kelp gull in Figure 1b is rounded up compared to Supplemental Figure 1 tree –
recommend consistency to avoid unnecessary confusion.
Figure S1 - “Sequences produced in the study are highlighted in bold red” in Figure 1, but not Supplemental Figure 1 –
could both be highlighted for consistency.
Figure S1 - The posterior probabilities are a bit difficult to read / match with the branch because of the overlap. I am not sure
how to solve this. Maybe the ones corresponding to samples from this study could be bolded? For instance, for the seal, it is
difficult to see if it is 0.9 or 0.3.
Table 1 - As you use a, b, & c to refer to positive samples in the Results section, you could consider adding the a, b, & c
labels in Table 1.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript presents the first genomic detections of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b
(genotype B3.2) in Antarctica. Until very recently—apart from the sub-Antarctic outbreaks described by Banyard et al. (2024,
Nat Commun)—the Antarctic continent appeared free of HPAI H5N1. The authors now provide whole-genome sequences
from three hosts (kelp gull, pintado petrel, Antarctic fur seal) collected during the 2023/24 and 2024/25 austral summers
within the Antarctic Treaty area (> 60° S).
The study is timely, novel, and ecologically important: it documents multiple independent virus introductions into previously
naïve wildlife populations, including a marine mammal. The methods are rigorous, the writing is clear, and the conclusions
are well supported. The work will interest epidemiologists, virologists, and conservation biologists alike.
The rapid spread of the ongoing H5N1 panzootic into the Southern Hemisphere – reaching South America in late 2022 and
the sub-Antarctic islands (e.g., Falklands, South Georgia) by late 2023 which has been supported by the report from CDC–
raised serious concerns about introduction into Antarctic ecosystems. This study now provides the first confirmed whole-
genome sequences of H5N1 from within the Antarctic Treaty region (>60°S), collected during the 2023/24 and 2024/25
austral summers from a kelp gull, a pintado petrel, and an Antarctic fur seal. The work is highly significant ecologically, as it
documents the incursion of HPAI into previously naïve wildlife populations (including both seabirds and a marine mammal).
The manuscript is very well-written and the findings are presented clearly. Overall, the study’s timeliness, novelty, and
potential conservation importance are commendable. It will be of great interest to epidemiologists, virologists, and wildlife
health experts.
The manuscript appropriately cites Banyard et al., which first reported H5N1 incursions in South Georgia and the Falklands,
and it makes clear that this study extends those observations to the Antarctic continent itself. In summary, the results are
robust, the conclusions are well-supported, and the work represents a valuable and novel contribution. I have only minor
suggestions detailed below:
1- Clarify the comparison with Banyard et al. (2024): In the Introduction and Discussion, the authors should more explicitly
position their findings relative to the prior report by Banyard et al. I suggest the authors clearly state how their results extend
or differ from Banyard et al.’s findings. A clearer comparison will help readers appreciate the advancement this work
represents and the continuity of the epidemiological narrative. Emphasizing the distinct introduction via South Georgia vs.
direct South American lineages, as uncovered here, would also strengthen the discussion of routes.
2- Mammalian adaptation markers – consider adding a summary table: Given that one of the isolates comes from a
mammalian host (an Antarctic fur seal), the manuscript should address whether any known mammalian-adaptive mutations
are present in these viral genomes. The authors do note in the text that no unusual adaptations were observed, which is
reassuring. To reinforce this point, it would be useful to explicitly report the presence or absence of key mutations associated
with mammalian adaptation or increased virulence.
3- Minor editing points: The manuscript is generally very well written. I did not find significant typos or errors. The flow of the
text is logical and concise. If not already done, a quick proofread for any minor grammatical issues or consistency (e.g., in
nomenclature of gene segments or clades) would be worthwhile.

number of HPAIV-infected species increased from 3 to 7. The expanded dataset improves
the robustness of our analyses and supports our initial conclusion of multiple independent

revised phylogenetic figures and supplementary materials.

A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b (genotype B3.2) in Antarctica. Until very recently—apart from the

R2- NCOMMS-25-38772A
We are once again very grateful for the reviewers’ constructive feedback. Below,
we provide our point-by-point responses to all comments and suggestions.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Comment: The inclusion of additional sampling and sequencing has somewhat
improved this paper. But there are still major flaws with the genetic analysis.
In the phylogenetic trees there are long branches leading into the sequences from
Antarctica that represent over 1 year of evolution. My previous suggestion to
expand the geographic origin of the viruses included in the phylogeny was partly
from concern that the analysis might be missing links to viruses from other
locations apart from South America (although this is the most logical source). I
would still prefer to see a phylogeny (perhaps just limited to the concatenated
genome) that includes a globally representative dataset. This could be easily
done with Nextstrain and would most likely address my concern and support the
restriction of the genetic analysis to South American strains.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important observation. With regards to
the long branches of the phylogenetic trees, this is unfortunately due to the gaps
in sampling and also reflects the inherent limitations of the Antarctic region.
Antarctica is an unusual ecosystem with extreme seasonality, being almost
completely abandoned by wildlife (with rare exceptions that breed in winter such
as emperor penguins, which are absent from our study area) and virtually
inaccessible to researchers during winter (hence even environmental sampling
would be hardly feasible). It is only feasible to obtain samples in spring/summer
and there is an unavoidable data gap in autumn/winter. Because our phylogenetic
trees are time-calibrated, this dynamic visually translates into unusually long
branches. Hence, while in other epidemiological systems the existence of long
branches in the phylogenetic trees could be interpreted as a red flag that indicates
failures in surveillance/sequencing effort, in the Antarctic context these long
branches are not unexpected and are virtually impossible to avoid.
With regards to the restriction of the genetic analysis to South American,
Subantarctic and Antarctic strains, there is some background that is worth
considering. Previous studies have established that, with the exception of a few
initial introductions to Colombia and Venezuela that were unsuccessful, all strains
that disseminated throughout South America originated from a single introduction
of clade 2.3.4.4b genotype B3.2 from North America to Peru in October 2022
(Leguía et al. 2023; Ospina-Jimenez et al. 2024; Uhart et al. 2024; Bruno et al.
2025; Pardo-Roa et al. 2025; Uhart & Vanstreels 2025). And, more importantly,
none of the strains detected to date in the Subantarctic/Antarctic region have
shown association with strains from continents other than South America.
Furthermore, all virus sequenced in South America in 2023 and 2024 show no
evidence of genomic reassortment, and all were directly descendent from this
initial October 2022 introduction, retaining the genotype B3.2 (Rimondi et al.
2025; Vanstreels et al. 2025). Genomic analyses corroborate that all viruses in
that region descended from South American strains and retained the B3.2
genotype (Banyard et al. 2024; Clessin et al. 2025). Our data and that of McCulley
et al. 2025 show that the same is true for the viruses that spread onto Antarctica,
i.e. all Subantarctic/Antarctic HPAI viruses sequenced thus far were descendants
of the introduction to South America dating back to October 2022. Specifically,
this is demonstrated by our phylogenetic trees for each gene segment (trees in
Supplementary File 4), which show how all Subantarctic/Antarctic virus
sequences are placed well within the clade of South American viruses, with high
statistical support and highly consistent tree structures across all eight gene
segments as well as in the concatenated genome (Supplementary File 3).
Nevertheless, in response to the reviewer’s concern, we have added a new
maximum likelihood tree for the HA gene of >800 sequences of globally
representative strains of the H5 clade 2.3.4.4b. This analysis has been included
in the supplementary materials (new Supplementary File 2), and offers a further
demonstration that all Subantarctic and Antarctic viruses descend from South
American viruses.
Literature cited in the response:
Banyard et al. 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-51490-8
Bruno et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virol.2025.110602
Clessin et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64297-y
Leguía et al. 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-41182-0
McCulley et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.1128/mra.00041-25
Ospina-Jimenez et al. 2024 https://doi.org/10.3389/fvets.2024.1347509
Pardo-Roa et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57338-z
Rimondi et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-7960151/v1
Vanstreels et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.05.23.655175
Uhart et al. 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-53766-5
Uhart & Vanstreels 2025 https://doi.org/10.1139/cjm-2025-0189
Comment: The authors say that they have conducted a phylogeographic
analysis, but there is no actual presentation of the phylogeography results in the
manuscript. It is inexplicable, particularly as transmission dynamics would be
informative for this study. There are no statistical supports provided in Figure 3,
there are lines drawn on a map that represent phylogenetic relationships from the
trees. Unfortunately these results would also be subject to sampling biases in the
datasets, a well known problem with phylogeography, none of which is discussed.
Response: Fair enough, our previous description may have incorrectly implied
that a formal phylogeographic analysis had been performed when this is not the
case. In reality, what we did was a phylogenetic analysis that incorporates a
discrete phylogeographic model, which is not the same as a phylogeographic
analysis sensu stricto. We edited the sub-heading of the Methods were this was
implied to correct this.
With regards to Figure 3, we should clarify that our intention was not to present a
statistical phylogeographic reconstruction, but rather to provide a conceptual
visualization of the putative routes of HPAI H5N1 spread in the Subantarctic and
Antarctic regions. The arrows in this figure are drawn from formal
phylogeographic reconstructions performed by other studies (Banyard et al.
2024; Uhart et al. 2024; Clessin et al. 2025) and from inference based from
phylogenetic analyses in this and previous studies (McCulley et al. 2025;
Steinfurth et al. 2025). By integrating our findings with those of earlier studies we
believe this figure will help readers better understand the geographic context
(distances and positions of the various Subantarctic islands and study sites) and
potential pathways of spread that are being discussed in text. It is true that this
figure is subject to limitations related to geographic sampling biases, however this
is the case of everything else in this and other studies, it is a recurring challenge
in all research of HPAI viruses in the Subantarctic and Antarctic region, and it is
something that we already mention in the Discussion.
In response to the reviewer’s concerns, we edited the caption of Figure 3 to clarify
that the map does not represent a phylogeographic analysis per se but instead is
a conceptual representation integrating the works of others and our own
phylogenetic analysis. The caption now reads as follows:
“Figure 3. Conceptual representation of the hypothesized pathways of
spread of HPAIV H5N1 in the Subantarctic and Antarctic region, based on
the findings of this study and prior studies that performed phylogeographic
and phylogenetic reconstruction5,7,13,27,28. Arrows represent the potential
routes of spatial dissemination of the HPAIV H5N1 South American
“marine mammal” (blue) and “avian” (red) sub-clades (sensu Uhart and
colleagues5).”
Literature cited in the response:
Banyard et al. 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-51490-8
Clessin et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64297-y
McCulley et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.1128/mra.00041-25
Steinfurth et al. 2025 https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.09.06.674618
Uhart et al. 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-53766-5
Comment: The structure of the paper could be improved. There is a very small
results section and then 5 pages of discussion that includes a rehashing of the
results. In my opinion the manuscript requires reorganization. The "Conservation
and management implications" could form the bulk of the discussion with
everything prior to that under results.
Response: We appreciate the constructive comment regarding the manuscript
structure. To our understanding, the Results section presents the findings of a
study in a strictly objective approach (i.e. the results of the experiment in a
vaccuum), whereas the Discussion section interprets these findings in light of the
literature and discussing hypotheses that may explain them (i.e. the experiment
under the light of human knowledge). This is of course a subjective and
somewhat nuanced distinction that also reflects stylistic preferences and
academic traditions across different fields of research and cultures. Nevertheless,
we feel this approach is well suited to the scope of this study and, in our
experience, it has been the most adopted in the biological literature.
In this sense, we would prefer to keep the text that is under the sub-headings
"Dissemination of “marine mammal” viruses from South America to Antarctica"
and "Virus dissemination through South Georgia as a ‘stepping stone’"
and "Genomic features" in the Discussion rather than moving it to the Results. This is
because in those sections we are taking information that was objectively
presented in the Results and interpreting it in light of other studies and collective
human knowledge, proposing hypothesis to explain them and drawing
implications to our broader understanding of the ecology and evolution of HPAI
viruses. Nevertheless, because we understand this is a stylistic choice, if the
editors disagree and would like us to restructure our Results and Discussion
sections as suggested by the reviewer or in another way that the editors feel
would be more suitable to the journal, please let us know and we can do so.
Comment: Overall this study lacks significance due to flawed genetic analyses.
Response: We respectfully disagree. Of course the study has flaws, such as the
limited sample size when compared to studies on poultry or on wildlife in less
remote regions of the world, or the limited availability of regional sequencing data
to strengthen the phylogenetic inferrence that can be drawn from our sequences.
However, we feel that given the practical challenges of collecting samples in
Antarctica, our study provides a robust contribution to the literature and to our
current understanding of HPAI viruses in Antarctic wildlife.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Comment: The manuscript has been considerably improved through revision,
including notably larger sample sizes, and more appropriate and better explained
methods. I really appreciate the paragraph on oral vs fecal shedders, which will
help guide future work on HPAI in wildlife. The conclusions are now well
supported by the manuscript.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment of our revised
manuscript.
Comment: Line 128 - I am confused about whether this motif was found in 1 ("an")
or 3 ("3 complete genomes [from the same individual?]") fur seals.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity. This motif was
detected in only one Antarctic fur seal. We recovered three complete genomes
from this same individual, obtained from the nasal, oral, and brain samples, and
all of them exhibited the PLKEKRRKRGLF motif.
We revised the text as follows, which should convey this more clearly:
“The original PLREKRRKRGLF motif was found in most viruses from both
phylogenetic groups, comprising 14 complete genomes and 5 partial
genomes. However, the PLKEKRRKRGLF motif was detected in group “a”
viruses recovered from three hosts: one Antarctic fur seal (three complete
genomes from the same individual), one Antarctic tern (one partial
genome), and one Antarctic petrel (one partial genome) (Supplementary
File 6).”
Comment: Line 162 - It is not obvious to me why multiple introductions would be
more conservative than diversification.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out, the text was incorrect. We agree with
the reviewer that it is more conservative to assume less, not more, introduction
events, but when writing this paragraph we failed to convey this. Furthermore,
during drafting we had gone back and forth about the best approach to interpret
the discrepancies among the different phylogenetic analyses, and this caused
some parts of the text to become incongruent.
When it comes to the strains of the group “a”, some of our phylogenetic analyses
pointed to there having been 4 introduction events (concatenated genome),
others pointed to 3 introduction events (PB2, PB1, PA, HA, and NP) and others
pointed to 2 introduction events (NA and NS). In this sense, we consider it more
“conservative” to consider that there were less introduction events, i.e. the
hypothesis of local diversification is more conservative than the hypothesis of
additional introductions. And therefore our more “conservative” interpretation is
that there were only 2 introduction events in group “a”. Adding to the other
introduction event that led to group “b”, we feel that our study provides robust
evidence for 3 introduction events in total.
On this basis and in consideration of the reviewer’s comments, we made minor
edits to Figure 3 and to the Abstract to reflect this interpretation. Furthermore, the
paragraph of the Discussion was revised and now reads as follows:
“Our analyses suggest that group “a” strains recovered from Antarctic
wildlife were polyphyletic; however, different analytical methods disagreed
on the number of introduction events that might have originated them. All
analyses agreed that the virus from the kelp gull sampled at Livingston
Island in January 2024 (individual O2601) was clearly distinct from the
remaining group “a” strains, representing an isolated introduction event.
However, the analyses disagreed on whether the remaining group “a”
strains resulted from multiple introduction events or not. Hence, until
further data is available to corroborate additional introduction events, we
conservatively consider that the group “a” strains detected in this study
descended from only two separate introduction events. Future genomic
data from South American, Antarctic and Subantarctic HPAIV H5N1
viruses may help clarifying the number of introduction events and whether
they occurred directly from South America or indirectly via Subantarctic
islands. In particular, it is worth noting that one of the strains recovered
from Antarctic fur seal (individual O2913) at King George Island in
December 2024 was closely related to a strain from a southern fulmar
(Fulmarus glacialoides) sampled in the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands in
October 2023, hinting at the possibility that the archipelago may have
served as a “stepping stone”.”
Comment: Line 184 (or somewhere else in the discussion) - I would add a
mention about unsampled species here, which could also have played a role in
the dissemination of the virus, such a fulmars and giant petrels, which have been
observed to carry the virus and suspected to play a role in its dissemination
(Banyard et al. 2024; Clessin et al. 2025), but can be harder to access, or less
likely to die, than the sampled species. I do not mean listing all potential species,
but only acknowledging that we only observe part of the process, notably because
some species are more difficult to access.
Response: Thank you for this suggestion. We agree that the role of unsampled
species in the dissemination of HPAIV H5N1 is an important point that should be
acknowledged. In response to this comment, we have added the following
sentence to the Discussion acknowledging that our observations represent only
a subset of the ecological process, as some key species are difficult to sample or
detect:
“It is also important to acknowledge the potential role of other birds species
as fulmars and giant petrels—both of which have been reported as
infected or suspected to participate in HPAIV H5N1 spread7,27—were not
sampled in this study, either because they are locally less abundant,
experienced less mortality, or are less likely to be detected as carcasses.”
Comment: Line 265 - I would suggest spelling out SSAFS each time as the
abbreviation is used only a few times.
Response: Done.
Comment: Line 338 - In the response, the authors talk about an asymmetric
model but I only see mentions of the symmetric model in the manuscript.
Response: Thank you for drawing attention to this inconsistency. We confirm that
the phylogeographic analyses presented in the manuscript were conducted using
a symmetric discrete CTMC diffusion model, as correctly described in the
Methods. The mention to an asymmetric diffusion model in our response to a
comment in the first review round resulted from miscommunication between the
coauthors, leading to an imprecise wording in the response letter.
We should clarify that the use of a symmetric discrete phylogeographic model
does not imply an assumption of bidirectional or non-directional viral spread, but
rather reflects a conservative prior structure in which transition rates between
locations are assumed to be equal a priori. Although epidemiological and
ecological evidence suggests that HPAIV was predominantly spreading
southwards during the study period, the availability of sequence data from the
Subantarctic and Antarctic region remains limited and unevenly distributed
across locations. Under such conditions, the use of a symmetric model is
commonly recommended to avoid overparameterization and identifiability issues
that may arise when fitting asymmetric diffusion models with sparse data.
Importantly, despite this conservative modeling choice, the inferred spatial
dynamics consistently support a southward dissemination of HPAIV from South
America to Antarctica or to South Georgia and subsequently into Antarctica. This
directionality emerges from the posterior reconstruction of ancestral locations and
TMRCA estimates, rather than being imposed by directional priors.
We have revised the Methods section to clarify the rationale for adopting a
symmetric diffusion model. We apologize for any confusion this may have caused
and appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The spread of high pathogenic avian influenza virus (HPAIV) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into Antarctica poses a major threat to polar wildlife. We report the detection of H5N1 in carcasses of eight species during the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 austral summers in the South Shetland Islands: Antarctic shag, Antarctic tern, kelp gull, pintado petrel, Antarctic petrel, skuas, Antarctic fur seal, and southern elephant seal. Whole-genome sequencing, mutational profiling, and phylogenetic reconstruction revealed that the viruses detected in these hosts descended from distinct introduction events. One group of strains including complete and partial viral genomes from a gull, skuas, fur seals, an Antarctic tern, and a southern elephant seal clustered with H5N1 strains previously detected in marine mammals in South America and formed a polyphyletic lineage consistent with at least two independent introductions into Antarctica. A second group of strains including complete and partial viral genomes from petrels, shags, and skuas clustered with H5N1 strains previously detected in seabirds and marine mammals in South Georgia and with a previously reported HPAIV detection from Torgersen Island, Antarctic Peninsula. These findings reveal extensive epidemiological connectivity between South America and Antarctica, with South Georgia serving as a “stepping stone” for virus spread in the region.

---

## Introduction

Global spread of the high pathogenicity avian influenza virus (HPAIV) subtype H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b has caused unprecedented mortality among wild animals1. In late 2022, viruses of the B3.2 genotype were introduced to the Pacific coast of South America, disseminating rapidly and causing outbreaks in poultry and wildlife2–4. Phylogenetic reconstruction reveals that shortly after arrival to South America these viruses diverged into two sub-clades: an “avian” sub-clade that spread inland and was detected predominantly in poultry and terrestrial wild birds, and a “marine mammal” sub-clade that spread coastally and was detected predominantly in marine mammals and seabirds5,6. In October and November 2023, HPAIV H5N1 spread from South America onto the Subantarctic region, causing outbreaks in seabirds and marine mammals in South Georgia and Falkland (Malvinas) Islands7. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the viruses from South Georgia were monophyletic, descending from the South American “avian” sub-clade, whereas the strains from the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands were polyphyletic, descending from the South American “marine mammal” sub-clade7.

As the virus disseminated in wildlife in South America and South Georgia, concerns were raised that it could spread further onto the Antarctic Peninsula8,9. The first reports of wildlife mortality suspected to be due to HPAIV H5N1 in the Antarctic region were made in December 202310, and several confirmed detections have been made along the Antarctic Peninsula since then10–13. During the austral summers of 2023/2024 and 2024/2025, we collected swabs and tissue samples from deceased wildlife in the South Shetland Islands, Antarctic Peninsula, to perform molecular testing and genomic characterization of HPAIV H5N1.

---

## Results

We tested tissue and swab samples from 31 carcasses from 11 species (Supplementary Table 1), with 18 carcasses from 8 species testing positive for H5 influenza A virus: Antarctic shag (Leucocarbo bransfieldensis), Antarctic tern (Sterna vittata), kelp gull (Larus dominicanus), pintado petrel (Daption capense), Antarctic petrel (Thalassoica antarctica), skua (Stercorarius sp.), Antarctic fur seal (Arctocephalus gazella), and southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina). In total, 18 complete genomes (from 12 individuals) and 7 partial genomes (from 6 individuals) were recovered (Table 1). A maximum likelihood tree for the HA gene segment including globally-representative Gs/Gd clade 2.3.4.4b strains during 2021–2024 revealed that all viruses detected in the Subantarctic and Antarctic region to date stem from the viruses that circulated in South America since 2022 (Supplementary Figure 1). Furthermore, all complete genomes were of the H5N1 subtype with the B3.2 genotype; partial genomes were also in agreement with this classification.

Phylogenetic reconstructions of the concatenated whole genomes indicated the viruses recovered in this study belong to two clearly distinct groups, “a” and “b” (Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 2). Phylogenetic group “a” comprised 10 complete genomes (recovered from 3 Antarctic fur seals, 1 kelp gull, and 3 skuas) that clustered with viruses previously detected predominantly in marine mammals in South America (i.e. the South American “marine mammal” sub-clade2). Sequence identity suggests that 6 partial genomes (recovered from 1 Antarctic tern, 2 skuas, 1 Antarctic petrel, 1 southern elephant seal) were also part of this group. Phylogenetic reconstruction of concatenated whole genomes suggestRed that this group could be further divided into four subgroups, each potentially descending from a separate introduction event to Antarctica (Figure 1a). However, separate phylogenetic analysis of the longer gene segments (PB2, PB1, PA, HA, NP) only corroborated three subgroups, whereas analysis of the shorter gene segments only corroborated one (MP) or two subgroups (NA, NS) (Supplementary Figure 3).

On the other hand, phylogenetic group “b” (Figure 1b) comprised 8 complete genomes (recovered from 1 Antarctic shag, 1 pintado petrel, and 3 skuas) clustered with viruses previously detected in seabirds and marine mammals from South Georgia and with a previously reported HPAIV detection in a brown skua (Stercorarius antarcticus) from Torgersen Island in Antarctica, which in turn descended from viruses that circulated in poultry and wild birds in South America (i.e. the South American “avian” sub-clade2). ## Paper

## Abstract

The spread of high pathogenic avian influenza virus (HPAIV) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b into Antarctica poses a major threat to polar wildlife. We report the detection of H5N1 in carcasses of eight species during the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 austral summers in the South Shetland Islands: Antarctic shag, Antarctic tern, kelp gull, pintado petrel, Antarctic petrel, skuas, Antarctic fur seal, and southern elephant seal. Whole-genome sequencing, mutational profiling, and phylogenetic reconstruction revealed that the viruses detected in these hosts descended from distinct introduction events. One group of strains including complete and partial viral genomes from a gull, skuas, fur seals, an Antarctic tern, and a southern elephant seal clustered with H5N1 strains previously detected in marine mammals in South America and formed a polyphyletic lineage consistent with at least two independent introductions into Antarctica. A second group of strains including complete and partial viral genomes from petrels, shags, and skuas clustered with H5N1 strains previously detected in seabirds and marine mammals in South Georgia and with a previously reported HPAIV detection from Torgersen Island, Antarctic Peninsula. These findings reveal extensive epidemiological connectivity between South America and Antarctica, with South Georgia serving as a “stepping stone” for virus spread in the region.

---

## Introduction

Global spread of the high pathogenicity avian influenza virus (HPAIV) subtype H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b has caused unprecedented mortality among wild animals1. In late 2022, viruses of the B3.2 genotype were introduced to the Pacific coast of South America, disseminating rapidly and causing outbreaks in poultry and wildlife2–4. Phylogenetic reconstruction reveals that shortly after arrival to South America these viruses diverged into two sub-clades: an “avian” sub-clade that spread inland and was detected predominantly in poultry and terrestrial wild birds, and a “marine mammal” sub-clade that spread coastally and was detected predominantly in marine mammals and seabirds5,6. In October and November 2023, HPAIV H5N1 spread from South America onto the Subantarctic region, causing outbreaks in seabirds and marine mammals in South Georgia and Falkland (Malvinas) Islands7. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the viruses from South Georgia were monophyletic, descending from the South American “avian” sub-clade, whereas the strains from the Falkland (Malvinas) Islands were polyphyletic, descending from the South American “marine mammal” sub-clade7.

As the virus disseminated in wildlife in South America and South Georgia, concerns were raised that it could spread further onto the Antarctic Peninsula8,9. The first reports of wildlife mortality suspected to be due to HPAIV H5N1 in the Antarctic region were made in December 202310, and several confirmed detections have been made along the Antarctic Peninsula since then10–13. During the austral summers of 2023/2024 and 2024/2025, we collected swabs and tissue samples from deceased wildlife in the South Shetland Islands, Antarctic Peninsula, to perform molecular testing and genomic characterization of HPAIV H5N1.

---

## Results

We tested tissue and swab samples from 31 carcasses from 11 species (Supplementary Table 1), with 18 carcasses from 8 species testing positive for H5 influenza A virus: Antarctic shag (Leucocarbo bransfieldensis), Antarctic tern (Sterna vittata), kelp gull (Larus dominicanus), pintado petrel (Daption capense), Antarctic petrel (Thalassoica antarctica), skua (Stercorarius sp.), Antarctic fur seal (Arctocephalus gazella), and southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina). In total, 18 complete genomes (from 12 individuals) and 7 partial genomes (from 6 individuals) were recovered (Table 1). A maximum likelihood tree for the HA gene segment including globally-representative Gs/Gd clade 2.3.4.4b strains during 2021–2024 revealed that all viruses detected in the Subantarctic and Antarctic region to date stem from the viruses that circulated in South America since 2022 (Supplementary Figure 1). Furthermore, all complete genomes were of the H5N1 subtype with the B3.2 genotype; partial genomes were also in agreement with this classification.

Phylogenetic reconstructions of the concatenated whole genomes indicated the viruses recovered in this study belong to two clearly distinct groups, “a” and “b” (Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 2). Phylogenetic group “a” comprised 10 complete genomes (recovered from 3 Antarctic fur seals, 1 kelp gull, and 3 skuas) that clustered with viruses previously detected predominantly in marine mammals in South America (i.e. the South American “marine mammal” sub-clade2). Sequence identity suggests that 6 partial genomes (recovered from 1 Antarctic tern, 2 skuas, 1 Antarctic petrel, 1 southern elephant seal) were also part of this group. Phylogenetic reconstruction of concatenated whole genomes suggestRed that this group could be further divided into four subgroups, each potentially descending from a separate introduction event to Antarctica (Figure 1a). However, separate phylogenetic analysis of the longer gene segments (PB2, PB1, PA, HA, NP) only corroborated three subgroups, whereas analysis of the shorter gene segments only corroborated one (MP) or two subgroups (NA, NS) (Supplementary Figure 3).

On the other hand, phylogenetic group “b” (Figure 1b) comprised 8 complete genomes (recovered from 1 Antarctic shag, 1 pintado petrel, and 3 skuas) clustered with viruses previously detected in seabirds and marine mammals from South Georgia and with a previously reported HPAIV detection in a brown skua (Stercorarius antarcticus) from Torgersen Island in Antarctica, which in turn descended from viruses that circulated in poultry and wild birds in South America (i.e. the South American “avian” sub-clade2). Sequence identity suggests that one partial genome (recovered from Antarctic shag) was also part of this group. This group was consistently monophyletic across all phylogenetic reconstructions (Supplementary Figures 2 and 3), suggesting that these viruses and the Torgersen Island virus descended from a single introduction event to Antarctica.

A comparison of cycle threshold (Ct) values of the Real Time RT-PCR revealed that birds could be classified as either oral shedders, which had higher viral loads (i.e. lower Ct values) in the oropharyngeal swabs than in the cloacal swabs, or fecal shedders, which had higher viral loads in cloacal swabs than in oropharyngeal swabs. Birds infected with group “a” strains were more frequently oral shedders (2 skuas, 1 tern) than fecal shedders (1 skua), whereas birds infected with group “b” strains were more frequently fecal shedders (1 skua, 1 petrel) than oral shedders (1 skua) (Supplementary Figure 4).

Mutational analysis revealed amino acid substitutions that distinguished phylogenetic groups “a” and “b” across all proteins except M1 (Figure 2 and Supplementary Data 1). Most group “a” strains recovered from both birds and mammals showed two key mammalian adaptation substitutions in PB2 (PB2-Q591K and PB2-D701N); another mammalian adaptation substitution in NP (NP-N319K) was detected in a group “a” strain recovered from the brain of an Antarctic fur seal (individual O2904). All group “b” viruses had a deletion of 17 amino acids in the neuraminidase stalk (positions 58-74). Lastly, two amino acid motifs were observed in the hemagglutinin cleavage site. The original PLREKRRKRGLF motif was found in most viruses from both phylogenetic groups, comprising 14 complete genomes and 5 partial genomes. However, the PLKEKRRKRGLF motif was detected in group “a” viruses recovered from three hosts: one Antarctic fur seal (three complete genomes from the same individual), one Antarctic tern (one partial genome), and one Antarctic petrel (one partial genome) (Supplementary Table 2).

## Methods

Sample collection
This study was conducted in compliance with all relevant ethical and environmental regulations. No live animals were handled or sampled, as all biological material was obtained from carcasses. Research activities were carried out under license LW-20/24 issued by the Animal Use Ethics Committee of the Vice-Presidency for Research and Biological Collections (VPPCB), Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (Fiocruz). Sampling activities in Antarctica were authorized by the Environmental Assessment Group of the Brazilian Antarctic Program (PROANTAR). Fieldwork was conducted within the framework of the FIOANTAR and VIDEANTAR projects, with logistical support provided by the Brazilian Navy. All procedures followed strict biosafety protocols to ensure sample integrity and researcher safety. Supplementary Table 1 provides detailed information on the animals sampled. Oropharyngeal, oral, nasal, and cloacal swabs and brain tissue samples were collected in tubes with 1 mL of DNA/RNA Shield (Zymo Research, Irvine, USA) and stored at –80ºC. Samples were then transported with a strict cold-chain to the Laboratory of Respiratory Viruses, Exanthematous, Enteroviruses, and Viral Emergencies at the Oswaldo Cruz Institute (IOC) for further analysis.

RNA extraction and real-time RT-PCR
RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Cat. No. 52906) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Detection and subtyping of influenza A virus were performed by real-time RT-PCR using two assays: (i) the Biomanguinhos INFA/INFB/SC2 Multiplex Kit (ANVISA Registration No. 8014217006095), and (ii) the CDC Influenza A/B Typing Panel (Flu A/B Typing Kit, Cat. No. FluIVD03-6), targeting the matrix (InfA) and hemagglutinin (H5a and H5b) genes46,47 (Supplementary Data 1). H5a was developed to detect specific groups of H5 viruses of Asian origin (A/goose/Guangdong/1996 lineage and derivatives, which include many HPAI strains). H5b is complementary, covering genetic variations of H5 that could escape detection by the H5a assay. A viral load index was calculated for each sample by subtracting the Cycle threshold (Ct) value from 40.

Whole-genome sequencing and assembly
Whole-genome sequencing of positive samples was performed using a Multisegment Reverse Transcription-PCR (M-RT-PCR) amplification protocol48,49. The sequencing library was constructed using the COVIDSeq kit (Illumina, San Diego, USA). Sequencing was conducted on the MiSeq platform (Illumina), and genome assembly was carried out using the Iterative Refinement Meta-Assembler (IRMA) pipeline50. Clade classification was performed using NextClade v3.10.1 (https://clades.nextstrain.org/).

Bayesian evolutionary analysis
To place the viruses recovered from Antarctic wildlife in a global context, we downloaded 822 globally-representative HA gene sequences from Gs/Gd clade 2.3.4.4b viruses during 2021–2024 using NextStrain (https://nextstrain.org/). Phylogenetic relationships were inferred for the HA gene using the Maximum Likelihood methods available in IQ-Tree v. 2.4.0 with a GTR model of nucleotide substitution with gamma-distributed rate variation among sites. Publicly-available sequences of influenza A viruses from South America and Antarctica were obtained through Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data - GISAID (https://www.gisaid.org/) and GenBank (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nucleotide/) (Supplementary Data 2). Because this initial analysis confirmed that all Antarctic/Subantarctic strains were descendent from South American strains, subsequent evolutionary analyses omitted viruses from other continents. The temporal structure of the datasets in each segment was evaluated using TempEst v1.5.351 through a root-to-tip linear regression. The significance of the correlation between collection date and genetic distance was assessed using a Pearson correlation test, with adjustments for multiple comparisons made via the Benjamini–Hochberg method for false discovery rate control. Time-scaled phylogenetic trees were estimated using the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach implemented in BEAST v1.10.452, with BEAGLE v4.0.053 to improve computational efficiency. Bayesian trees were reconstructed under the nucleotide substitution model selected by jModelTest v2.1.1054, the non-parametric Bayesian Skyline coalescent demographic model55, and a relaxed molecular clock model with a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) rate reference prior56. The molecular clock, the time to the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA), and the spatial dynamics of each viral segment were reconstructed using a discrete phylogeographic model57 implemented in BEAST v1.10.4. A symmetric diffusion model was intentionally adopted as a conservative framework, allowing directional patterns of viral spread to emerge from the data rather than being imposed by prior assumptions, particularly given the limited and uneven geographic sampling in Antarctica.

In addition to segment-based analyses, concatenated gene datasets were also constructed and evaluated under the same Bayesian phylogeographic framework to capture genome-wide evolutionary signals. Sequences were coded according to both their sampling locations and host. For each dataset, independent MCMC runs were performed and subsequently combined to confirm that all continuous parameters achieved an effective sample size (ESS) greater than 100–200, as verified using Tracer v1.758. The maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree was summarized with TreeAnnotator v1.1052. Trees were visualized using R v4.4.159 with the packages treeio v1.30.060 and ggtree v3.14.061.

Mutational analysis
The translated sequence of all eight gene segments were compared to evaluate the presence of amino acid substitutions using NextClade v3.10.1 (https://clades.nextstrain.org/). An early B3.2 genotype strain (A/turkey/South Dakota/22-008485-001/2022; GISAID accession code EPI_ISL_11971481)62 was used as a reference.
